transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, nice to meet you, Dr. Smith. I'm here mostly because my family and everyone else keeps saying I've been doing too much lately. But to me... well, it honestly just feels like I'm the only one with enough drive to actually get things done. 

I mean, I'm getting our whole move handled, I'm rebuilding the new garage so it's done right, and I've been organizing things down at the church. And on top of all that, I'm still going in and showing the younger fellows at the plant how the grinding and blending jobs actually ought to be done. Somebody has to step up and do it. But they think it's a problem, so... here I am.
How long have you been feeling this way—full of energy, taking on all these projects, and needing less rest than usual?

Well, I'd say it's been going on for about a month now. It really started right around the time we were forced to start leaving the old house. There was just a lot to handle with all that, so I got to work.
Before this past month, have you ever gone through a period—lasting two weeks or more—where you felt unusually sad, down, or low on energy?

No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I haven't really had any times where I felt sad or low on energy like that. I've always been a pretty steady worker, you know? Just kept my head down and did what needed doing. I don't really get down in the dumps.

latest_inference.note: Patient denies any prior depressive episodes, and current presentation (elevated mood, decreased need for rest, increased goal-directed activity for ~1 month) is consistent with a single manic episode without psychotic features. This rules out F31.0/F31.1 (bipolar disorder, which requires at least one other mood episode) and F34.0 (cyclothymia, which involves chronic, less severe mood fluctuations rather than an acute manic episode).
